items.summary: Iran and Oman plan for temporary Hormuz corridor Iran has held new talks with neighbouring Oman on management of the Strait of Hormuz, blockaded over nearly six months of conflict, with Oman's foreign minister saying he was hopeful a temporary corridor through the waterway could be announced soon. Iran and Oman said on Tuesday that they discussed "a joint temporary navigational corridor" through the strait and agreed to clear it of mines. "I am hopeful we will soon announce a temporary corridor for the Strait of Hormuz and practical arrangements to restore safe navigation," Omani Foreign Minister Badr Albusaidi posted on X following talks with his Iranian counterpart. items.title: UN offers to facilitate fertiliser transit through Strait of Hormuz
items.summary: UN offers to facilitate fertiliser transit through Strait of Hormuz UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres offered on Monday to facilitate the transit of fertiliser through the Strait of Hormuz which has been disrupted as a result of the US-Israel war on Iran. “The purpose is simple: to reduce immediate risks, support more orderly and predictable transit and help rebuild the confidence necessary for diplomacy and de-escalation,” he said at a news conference. Guterres said the UN “would not authorise passage” through the strait or “alter the rights or obligations” of states under international law, but rather serve as a “neutral facilitator”, registering and verifying ships carrying fertiliser and related products. “Of course, it can only be done if the countries that are involved in this conflict all agree to accept the mechanism,” Guterres said, which would be coordinated by Oman.

items.summary: China warns US of retaliation over expansion of Iran sanctions China on Tuesday warned the US that it could retaliate if Washington expands its sanctions campaign against Iran to target Chinese companies, potentially opening a new front in tensions between the world’s two largest economies. The warning came after US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Monday announced measures aimed at further isolating Iran and threatening countries that continue to trade with Tehran with exclusion from the dollar-based financial system. The Financial Times reported that Beijing had warned against any significant extension of secondary sanctions to Chinese businesses, with a foreign ministry spokesperson saying that China would take “all necessary measures” to protect its interests. The spokesperson reiterated Beijing’s opposition to unilateral sanctions imposed without UN Security Council authorisation, while calling for de-escalation and a return to negotiations over the US-Iran conflict, according to the FT. items.summary: China warns US against expanding Iran sanctions to Chinese firms China has warned Washington that it will retaliate if the Trump administration significantly expands its Iran-related secondary sanctions against Chinese companies. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced measures on Monday targeting companies in mainland China and Hong Kong. Washington stopped short of sanctioning major Chinese financial institutions. “China will take all necessary measures to firmly safeguard its rights and interests,” a Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson said on Tuesday. “China has made clear on many occasions its firm opposition to illicit unilateral sanctions that have no basis in international law or the authorisation of the UN Security Council,” they said. “The pressing task is to facilitate de-escalation of the situation and return to dialogue and negotiation as soon as possible,” they added.

items.summary: Ante las dudas y críticas sobre el nuevo acuerdo petrolero de Donald Trump con Venezuela, su vicepresidente, J. D. Vance, salió este jueves en la Casa Blanca a defenderlo y a presentarlo como una pieza de la estrategia de Washington para blindar a EE.UU. frente a futuras crisis energéticas , en un momento de creciente beligerancia con Irán y de encarecimiento de los combustibles. Vance sostuvo que Washington no puede depender de que otros países garanticen el suministro mundial de energía y cargó además contra los aliados europeos, entre ellos España, por lo que describió como su incapacidad para responder con suficiente firmeza a las amenazas iraníes contra las rutas marítimas.La tesis del vicepresidente es que la apertura del sector petrolero venezolano permite a EE.UU. incorporar a los mercados una enorme reserva de crudo cercana geográficamente y reducir así la vulnerabilidad ante crisis como la actual con Irán. Según Vance, el acuerdo permitirá poner en explotación efectiva unos 65.000 millones de barriles de reservas mediante la entrada de compañías estadounidenses en Venezuela

clusters.headline: El último bandazo de Trump en Irán depende de China

items.title: El último bandazo de Trump en Irán depende de China
items.summary: En los últimos días y semanas, Trump y su Administración han obrado el último bandazo en la guerra contra el régimen de Teherán: una campaña económica que aísle todavía más a Irán de las finanzas globales y fuerce un acuerdo sobre su programa nuclear, el gran objetivo del presidente de EE.UU. El problema es que cumplir con ese plan tiene un problema: requiere de una confrontación directa con China, el gran sustento de Irán. Y Trump tendrá que hacer equilibrios entre lograr un verdadero aislamiento de Irán y no abrir un nuevo frente con Pekín.Trump y su secretario del Tesoro, Scott Bessent , han hablado de ello en las últimas semanas, en una indicación de su intención de dejar de lado -al menos, de momento- la presión militar y centrarse en la presión económica. Es el tercer giro del conflicto con Irán, que ha pasado de la guerra total a la ofensiva diplomática -sin gran éxito- y, ahora, a la presión económica. Una opción mucho más digerible que la militar para el votante estadounidense, también para el 'trumpismo', ahora que estamos a la vuelta de la esquina de las decisivas eleccion

"Iran now faces a very clear choice, with only two paths before them: complete global isolation and a subsistence economy, or a path back to normalcy with an opportunity to rejoin the global economy," Bessent told reporters in Washington, DC. It remains unclear how "a path to normalcy" may work, given the Trump administration has only ever tightened sanctions on Iran since its first iteration in the White House in 2017. "Today, we are launching Operation Economic Outcast to foreclose every other option available to the Iranian regime," Bessent declared. "America is no longer managing the Iranian threat. items.summary: Iran urges UN action over deadly US attack on wedding Iran has accused the United States of committing a “war crime” by bombing a wedding gathering in southern Hormozgan province. In a letter to the United Nations Security Council, Iranian Ambassador Gholamhossein Darzi described the attack on civilians as an “appalling” and “egregious” crime that violated international law. Darzi urged the UN to “hold the United States fully responsible” and ensure it brings “an end to its acts of aggression” against Iran. The US strike killed at least four people, including two children, and wounded 50 others at the wedding in Sirik. Iran’s Health Ministry said recent US air strikes had killed at least 18 people and wounded another 142.

Speaking on Monday before travelling to Bishkek for a Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit, Pezeshkian said Iran “is not looking for war” but would “never sit still in the face of any aggression”. Iran “will give a decisive response to the aggressors” if attacked again, he said, according to the Fars news agency. “Instability and unrest in the region are not in the interest of any country and will challenge everyone,” he added. US forces bombed Larak Island on Sunday, the official state broadcaster IRIB reported. It marked Washington’s first attack on Iran since July and raised fears of another escalation in the Israeli -US war against the country . clusters.headline: Did Trump put a poison pill in his own Saudi nuclear deal?

items.title: Did Trump put a poison pill in his own Saudi nuclear deal?
items.summary: This week, President Donald Trump formally submitted the U.S.-Saudi civil nuclear agreement to Congress for review, moving the deal forward despite continuing to insist that Saudi Arabia normalize relations with Israel before it can take effect. This condition could stall the agreement indefinitely: Riyadh demands a clear pathway toward Palestinian statehood before normalization, and Israel is dead set against statehood. Israel had strongly opposed the deal as originally negotiated, while Netanyahu had privately expressed hopes of delivering “ the next big thing ” by securing Saudi normalization before Israel’s October elections. Former U.S. Ambassador to Saudi Arabia Michael Ratney described Trump as inserting normalization “ at the last minute ,” throwing the agreement into uncertainty. Trump’s decision to submit the agreement for congressional review further adds to this uncertainty. The president appears to want it both ways: his latest move is signaling to Riyadh that the agreement is moving forward even as he assures Tel Aviv that the deal is contingent on normalization. items.summary: Iran says US sanctions will achieve nothing Iran's president insisted on Wednesday that the United States would achieve nothing with its new sanctions campaign after Washington laid out plans to collapse the country's economy. Almost six months into their war, the two sides are locked in a stalemate, with Iran keeping the key Strait of Hormuz shut and Washington persisting with a naval counter-blockade of Iran. "America will not achieve anything with economic pressure at this stage, just as it was unable to achieve anything in the war," Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said Wednesday, according to the country's ISNA news agency. "We will stand firm against economic pressures, as we have done so far and will continue to do."

In the letter, led by Illinois Senator Tammy Duckworth, the lawmakers wrote to committee chairman Roger Wicker requesting a public hearing with Defense Department leadership regarding the poor management across naval ships and regional bases. A cargo jet, meanwhile, may have struck a second drone shortly after takeoff, forcing an abrupt landing, and investigators found a third drone laden with military explosives nearby. clusters.headline: ‘I would rather die than return to France’: the brutal reality of the UK’s one in, one out scheme

items.summary: Aso and Baran fled Iran, crossed the Channel together and were both returned to France. After risking their lives to reach Britain again, the friends found themselves facing very different fates At the end of last year, two men fled Iran. Aso and Baran* were strangers at the time. The way their stories would cross, then diverge, reveals the cruel arbitrariness of the UK asylum system in general, and the government’s controversial one in, one out scheme in particular. Before he left Iran, Aso, 28, had converted from Islam to Christianity, putting his life in imminent danger. “I had to keep my conversion to Christianity a secret,” he says. “I knew if I was caught, I risked being executed by the Iranian regime … one of my relatives, who I trusted, paid smugglers to get me out last November.” Continue reading...

clusters.headline: 'Inappropriate to say': Trump may still be considering CIA-led uprising in Iran

items.title: 'Inappropriate to say': Trump may still be considering CIA-led uprising in Iran
items.summary: 'Inappropriate to say': Trump may still be considering CIA-led uprising in Iran US President Donald Trump on Wednesday said it "wouldn't be appropriate to say" if he would greenlight the CIA arming Iranians to encourage a violent uprising, a day after he asked on his TruthSocial account, "When are the Iranian people going to rise up and fight?" Trump was taking unscheduled questions in the Oval Office, after the US unleashed a barrage of strikes on Iran's southern coast on Tuesday, killing 18 people, including two children at a wedding. "Will you send the CIA in to arm Iranians?" a reporter asked the president. "I'd love to tell you that, but it wouldn't be appropriate to say," Trump responded. "But I mean, I understand their plight. They're being shot... They have close to 65,000 protesters killed." It remains unclear where that figure is sourced, given Trump has previously floated figures between 25,000 and 80,000 during the anti-government protests in Iran early this year. Read more: 'Inappropriate to say': Trump may still be considering CIA-led uprising in Iran

items.summary: This summer the Pentagon handed NATO members a questionnaire asking whether they support in part, “U.S. foreign policy priorities.” Dubbed a “loyalty test” in the press, it was seen by many Europeans as the most recent sign that the alliance is coming apart because of American petulance. Yet what is actually happening is that the U.S. is putting stress on an inherently flawed and now exhausted form of alliance politics. The roots of the present discord were planted not in the 2024 reelection of President Donald Trump, but in the moment of NATO's Cold War triumph thirty years earlier. items.summary: UN chief urges US, Iran to 'return urgently to diplomacy' after renewed attacks UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres on Wednesday expressed "grave concern" after renewed strikes between the US and Iran, and condemned all attacks against civilians. "The secretary-general is deeply alarmed by reports of civilian casualties, including a strike that reportedly hit a wedding ceremony in Iran," UN spokesperson Stephane Dujarric said during a news conference. "The secretary-general condemns all attacks against civilians," Dujarric said. "He recalls that all parties must respect their obligations under international humanitarian law, including the principles of distinction, proportionality, and precaution." He added that the UN chief urged Washington and Tehran to "return urgently to diplomacy," adding that a "comprehensive and durable settlement can be achieved only through dialog and negotiations".

Since the Memorandum of Understanding collapsed in July, the prospects for reviving it have deteriorated by the day. While Tehran publicly demands a return to the MOU, Trump’s current position is that even if Iran reopened the Strait of Hormuz, he would neither return to the agreement nor lift the blockade on Iran. And even in the unlikely event that he did, the MOU could not come back into force as long as Israel continues to bombard Lebanon. Iran is unlikely to accept an MOU minus Lebanon: its demand for a regional ceasefire is non-negotiable. And those differences have now grown dramatically more severe because of Trump’s nuclear agreement with Saudi Arabia. Daarnaast zouden er vier leden van de Iraanse Revolutionaire Garde zijn gedood en drie leden van de paramilitaire militie Basij. items.summary: Fair to say the current sell-off is international, but the PM has said little yet to make investors rethink the UK’s status It’s too soon to say the bond markets have turned on Andy Burnham. Tuesday’s spike in gilt yields, taking the UK’s 30-year borrowing costs to their highest level since 1998 , was part of an international sell-off of government debt . The main contributors are well known. The Iran war, by increasing the cost of energy, has overturned the comforting start-of-the-year thesis of falling global inflation and interest rates. A plunging Japanese yen has kicked away another assumed source of financial stability. The US treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, hasn’t calmed nerves with his solo, and so far futile, attempt to bring down US yields . Meanwhile, the early stage of the AI revolution is an exercise in issuing squillions of debt before long-term returns on capital can possibly be assessed meaningfully. Continue reading...

items.title: Oorlog Midden-Oosten leidt tot stuk meer aanvragen bij Nationaal Warmtefonds
items.summary: Het Nationaal Warmtefonds heeft tot nu toe al meer leningen verstrekt dan in heel 2025. Bij het fonds kunnen mensen geld lenen om hun huis te verduurzamen. Van januari tot en met augustus werden ruim 22.000 leningen verstrekt. In heel 2025 waren dat er 21.000. De lening wordt gebruikt voor bijvoorbeeld muur- en dakisolatie, isolerend glas of zonnepanelen. De piek heeft te maken met de oorlog in het Midden-Oosten, die de VS en Israël eind februari ontketenden met hun aanvallen op Iran. Als tegenzet gooide Iran de Straat van Hormuz dicht, de zeestraat waardoor tot die tijd een vijfde van de wereldwijde olie en aardgas werd vervoerd. Door die blokkade zijn de energieprijzen fors gestegen. "De piek was vanaf het moment dat de oorlog begon", vertelt Katinka Huiberts, bestuurslid bij het Nationaal Warmtefonds. "De aanvragen begonnen toen heel scherp te stijgen." Die stijging zette het hele voorjaar tot de zomer door, zegt Huiberts. items.summary: Army Secretary Dan Driscoll resigned this week, raising a flurry of questions about whether his departure is part of a larger political reordering that has pushed skeptics of President Donald Trump’s war policies to the margins. A long-time friend of Vice President JD Vance, Driscoll drew widespread praise for his efforts to modernize the Army. But he has clashed with Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, particularly over the latter’s firing of numerous senior military officials , including Army and Air Force generals and the Secretary of the Navy. Driscoll brought his concerns about these firings directly to Trump last week, who said he was unaware of how many officers had been purged, according to the Atlantic. clusters.headline: Gulf states struggle to recover economically after 6 months of war

items.title: Gulf states struggle to recover economically after 6 months of war
items.summary: The Persian Gulf’s extraordinary wealth has long rested on an assumption of stability. The past six months of war have shattered that certainty, exposing a fundamental weakness in Gulf economic models: producing oil and gas is only half the equation when infrastructure and access to global markets can be disrupted. Ports, airports, power grids, desalination plants, financial centers, and tourism hubs are all vulnerable to the same regional shocks. The energy sector is particularly exposed, with damaged oil and gas facilities potentially taking months or longer to repair. Yet restoring production may prove easier than restoring confidence that Gulf exports can reliably reach global markets. Each Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) state enters this new era from a different starting point. Qatar, Kuwait and Bahrain are particularly exposed because of their reliance on Gulf maritime routes, including the Strait of Hormuz. Oil prices, which had been trending down amid a lull in fighting, spiked on Monday. Brent, the international benchmark, was up 2.5 percent to trade at $90.35 per barrel. But Trump’s bombast contrasts with reports that the US is in no position to escalate the war. The heads of the US army, navy and air force, and the four-star commanders overseeing US operations throughout Europe, Asia and Latin America, warned Secretary of War Pete Hegseth that any prolonging of major operations would weaken the US’s ability to confront other foes, the Washington Post reported on Monday. items.title: Oil prices jump amid resumption of US-Iran clashes
items.summary: Oil prices jump amid resumption of US-Iran clashes Crude oil prices rose on Monday after the US attacked Iran's Larak Island, prompting Iran to retaliate in the first open fire between the two countries since July. Brent crude prices jumped over 2.5 percent on Monday alone, taking prices to $90.34 per barrel. The US-Israeli assault has caused oil prices to spike amid Iran's closure of the vital strait of Hormuz shipping lane, although prices are now far lower than at the height of hostilities earlier this year, when crude traded at upwards of $110 per barrel.

clusters.headline: Why the Gulf Monarchies Will Not Turn Away from the United States Despite the Iran War

items.title: Why the Gulf Monarchies Will Not Turn Away from the United States Despite the Iran War
items.summary: The signing on 7 August of the so-called Mecca Pact by Saudi Arabia, Türkiye and Pakistan again raises the question of whether the Gulf monarchies might seek to reduce their security dependence on the United States. The Gulf monarchies’ experience of the Iran war makes such a realignment appear plausible. Despite their decades-long partnership with Washington, they became targets of Iranian drone and missile attacks that caused considerable damage to the region’s energy infrastructure and severely disrupted energy exports, as the Strait of Hormuz was effectively closed. The Trump administration appears to have taken little account of their security interests . Nevertheless, three factors make an end to their close ties with Washington unlikely. Limits of realignment First, the Gulf monarchies have no viable alternative to the United States as a security guarantor. For all their differences in foreign and security policy, they share a common predicament: None of their other partners is willing or able to take Washington’s place. items.summary: Un ipotetico bombardamento dell’isola iraniana di Kharg: un serbatoio di stoccaggio del petrolio e una petroliera esplodono, ripresi dall’alto da un velivolo. Si tratta però di un video generato con l’intelligenza artificiale e condiviso dal presidente degli Stati Uniti, Donald Trump, su Truth Social, accompagnato da un post in cui si legge: «Kharg Island ridotta in mille pezzi!». Prima dell’inizio della guerra, l’isola di Kharg gestiva la maggior parte delle esportazioni petrolifere iraniane, rappresentando un nodo strategico per l’economia di Teheran. Dall’inizio del conflitto, Trump ha più volte minacciato di prendere il controllo dell’isola o di distruggerne le infrastrutture. ► Segui gli aggiornamenti in diretta del conflitto in Medio Oriente | LEGGI ANCHE Le mine a Hormuz e il petrolio iraniano: perché Trump attacca di nuovo | L'isola di Kharg, chiave del petrolio iraniano, e il dilemma di Trump: conquistare o distruggere?

clusters.headline: La modernité de l’Iranienne Forough Farrokhzâd, poétesse rebelle et lumineuse

items.title: La modernité de l’Iranienne Forough Farrokhzâd, poétesse rebelle et lumineuse
items.summary: Forough Farrokhzâd est l’une des plus grandes figures de la poésie iranienne du dernier siècle. Sa disparition brutale en 1967, à l’âge de 32 ans, fut une perte immense pour son pays, pour la littérature. Sa voix, « fusionnée dans les atomes du temps » comme elle l’a écrit, continue de se faire entendre à travers sa poésie sublime et tragique. « J’irai jusqu’au rivage du soleil » est le titre du volume en traduction française de ses poésies complètes, paru cette année dans la prestigieuse collection Poésie/Gallimard.

In a statement on Saturday evening, the Shin Bet confirmed that “there was a significant threat to harm Yair Netanyahu, and in light of this and after an assessment, a decision was made to urgently extract him along with his security team and return him to Israel”. items.summary: Iran parliament speaker says new regional pacts can 'herald a new stage’ Iran’s parliament speaker, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, has said that new regional treaties can herald a new stage in which Muslim neighbours rely on their own capacities rather than on foreigners, according to Tasnim News Agency. In his message Saturday to mark the Unity Week, Ghalibaf described new regional treaties and arrangements as a “new chapter” and stressed that unity among Muslims has “helped push back against hegemonic ambitions”, according to Tasnim News Agency. He said these treaties show that Muslim neighbours “can choose the path of cooperation and brotherhood”, rather than “pursuing exhausting rivalries”. Ghalibaf added that recent developments have demonstrated the benefits of Muslim unity, and expressed hope that the Muslim world “would move toward greater unity, independence, security and dignity, with Muslims determining their own future free from foreign interference”.

clusters.headline: Iran-backed Iraqi group sets 10 conditions for disarmament, including full US withdrawal

items.title: Iran-backed Iraqi group sets 10 conditions for disarmament, including full US withdrawal
items.summary: Iran-backed Iraqi group sets 10 conditions for disarmament, including full US withdrawal Kataib Sayyid al-Shuhada, an Iran -backed Iraqi armed group, said on Saturday it will only cooperate with efforts to bring weapons under state control if 10 conditions are met, including a complete withdrawal of US forces from Iraq. The group said US forces must fully withdraw by land, sea and air, that any American presence “under any title” must end, and that Iraqi airspace must not be used to launch attacks on neighbouring countries. It also called for full federal control over Iraqi territory, stronger Iraqi-operated air defences with advanced systems, and the withdrawal of Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK) fighters and Turkish troops from northern Iraq. It said that the PKK's presence gives Turkey a pretext for cross-border operations. The group, which has longstanding ties to Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), made its statement as the Iraqi government faces a 30 September deadline to bring all armed factions' weapons under state control.

items.summary: After six months of war, Iran’s leadership has coalesced around a hard core of military generals and clerics long entrenched in the ruling theocracy. They are ready for a potentially long confrontation with the US and determined to prevent any unrest at home. It’s a far cry from US President Donald Trump’s initial hopes of toppling the Islamic Republic and his subsequent claims that “regime change” had brought more compromising officials to the fore. items.summary: Ignore Iran, the Epstein files, and your wallet – not to mention Trump’s plummeting approval ratings Don’t mention the war! Or the economy, for that matter. Or the Epstein files. Or Natalie Harp. Or “affordability”, which, as Donald Trump recently said at a rally, is a word that was “never used” by the media before he took office. Best not to talk about anything that affects ordinary people or embarrasses the president, really. Instead, let’s all rejoice in Trump’s latest triumph: renaming Lake Ontario, which is shared by Canada and the US, as Lake America . On Thursday, Trump signed an executive order directing federal agencies to America-fy the lake’s name on US maps and documents, which is an excellent use of time and resources. I suppose we can at least be thankful that the president, who is trying to slap his own name on everything from airports to the Kennedy Center , didn’t decree that the body of water be called Lake Trump. items.title: Nog 400 schepen vast in Perzische Golf, Iran claimt controle over Straat van Hormuz
items.summary: Sinds het begin van de Iranoorlog een half jaar geleden liggen nog altijd 400 schepen vast in de Perzische Golf. Dat meldt de Internationale Maritieme Organisatie (IMO). Ook zitten nog 6000 opvarenden vast, zegt de organisatie. "Zes maanden na het begin van het conflict in het Midden-Oosten is de situatie in de Straat van Hormuz nog steeds onopgelost", aldus IMO's secretaris-generaal Arsenio Dominguez. De wereldwijde economische impact door verstoringen van handelsstromen voor olie, kunstmest en andere grondstoffen door de blokkade is groot, zegt Dominguez. Sinds het begin van het conflict noteerde de IMO minstens zeventig aanvallen op de internationale scheepvaart met negentien doden tot gevolg. De IMO-raad nam vorige maand een resolutie aan waarin wordt opgeroepen tot een "gecoördineerde en duurzame terugkeer naar onbelemmerde navigatie door de Straat van Hormuz". Iran claimt controle Vannacht claimde de Iraanse Revolutionaire Garde op Telegram dat Iran de volledige controle heeft over de Straat van Hormuz, waar voor het uitbreken van de oorlog 20 procent van de wereldwijde oliehan

items.title: Rachel Roddy’s recipe for saffron and tomato rice | A kitchen in Rome
items.summary: Laborious to harvest and extortionately priced, the sunset-coloured stigmas of the saffron crocus have an extraordinarily warm, pungent taste. Fortunately, however, a little goes a very long way … The saffron crocus has six lilac-purple flowers, three yellow stamens and three orange-red stigmas that extend beyond the petals like the wiry antennae of an insect. The thread-like stigmas have to be picked only by hand when the flowers are fully open, a laborious, finickety job that hasn’t changed much since ancient times. Then, to avoid the colour and flavour fading, the stigmas need to be dried very quickly, a process that reduces their weight by about 80%. Tens of thousands of fiery-looking filaments are required to produce half a kilogram of the dried threads, which make the “hay” or powder we know as saffron and explains the exorbitant cost. Fortunately, just a few threads of this precious spice go a long way. Native to Crete, Iran and south-west Asia, the saffron crocus has been cultivated since the dawn of civilisation for its medicinal properties, as well as for use in cosmetics,

items.title: The rise and fall of 'resistance' hero Alexander Vindman
items.summary: On paper, Alexander Vindman’s loss in last week’s Florida Democratic Senate was a shocking upset. After all, Vindman had a 16-to-1 fundraising advantage and far more national name recognition than the winner — progressive state Rep. Angie Nixon. But the results reflect more than one poorly-run campaign. Vindman is one of the most prominent faces of a bygone political era known as "Russia-gate" — a period which Democratic voters appear ready to leave behind. Just a few years ago, the idea of Vindman losing a Democratic primary would have been hard to imagine. The former director for European affairs on the National Security Council had emerged from Donald Trump’s first term as one of the most celebrated stars of the anti-Trump “Resistance” due to his role in the 2019 impeachment hearings. As contemporary profiles in major media outlets noted, he became, in the eyes of his supporters, a “ patriotic truth-teller ,” who was unafraid to confront power. One Democratic lawmaker, Rep. items.title: Trump's war and tariffs are having a nasty effect on interest rates
items.summary: Over the last month, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has engaged in two controversial and rare interventions in financial markets. The first came in early August when the U.S. Treasury joined the government of Japan in its efforts to strengthen the yen by buying the Japanese currency, taking a step it had last taken during the Asian Financial Crisis in 1998. And late last week, Bessent announced that the Treasury could double the amount of long-dated Treasuries that it will buy back from current holders. The theme that unites both interventions is a concern that the interest rates the U.S government is paying on its long-term debt (also known as bond yields) are rising too high and too fast, with 30-year U.S. Treasury bond yields reaching 5.3%, levels last seen in 2007. Last February, Bessent said the administration was focused on lowering bond yields. items.summary: Iran-Oman Hormuz agreement not yet finalised: Iranian source Iran and Oman are still finalising an agreement on shares of the Strait of Hormuz and its revenues, Reuters is reporting, citing a senior Iranian source. According to the source, the countries are still working on the details of the agreement. This comes shortly after Iranian media, citing an IRGC spokesman, reported that the two countries had "reached results that have been accepted by both sides". In comments carried by Tasnim news agency, the spokesman confirmed that: “Agreements have been reached on the share of each country in the waters of the strait and the share of Iran and Oman in its revenues."

The US slapped 50% tariffs on another $20bn of Canadian goods – then threatened the same rate on the cars, trucks, parts and steel that America Inc depends on. On Monday, the Treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, menaced Iran’s trading partners with exclusion from the US financial network, hoping that coercion can deliver what months of war have not. And as the costs of war, tariffs and pro-billionaire tax cuts helped send US bond yields higher, the Treasury stepped in to tame long-term rates. clusters.headline: Iranians queue for petrol after US announces new sanctions

items.title: Iranians queue for petrol after US announces new sanctions
items.summary: Iranians queue for petrol after US announces new sanctions Long queues formed at petrol stations across Tehran on Tuesday after the United States announced fresh sanctions targeting Iran, AFP reported. The new measures come as Washington seeks to increase economic pressure on Tehran after six months of war that has reached a military stalemate, with peace talks stalled and most traffic through the strategically important Strait of Hormuz blocked. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Monday outlined plans for what he called the “economic asphyxiation” of Iran, saying the objective was to “sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime”. According to AFP, Iranian authorities have largely shrugged off Washington’s threats, noting that the country has lived under US sanctions for decades. But residents in Tehran expressed concern that the latest measures could further affect fuel supplies and the wider economy. The queues at petrol stations came amid growing uncertainty over fuel availability and prices as the latest US measures add to economic pressure on Iran.

De twee schepen gisteren waren een grote gastanker en een grote olietanker. Waardoor het aantal schepen zo sterk is gedaald, is niet duidelijk. Wellicht waren het er meer dan twee, omdat sommige schepen hun navigatiesystemen uitschakelen tijdens de passage. Iran heeft ondertussen 45 tankers op een zwarte lijst gezet wegens vermeende overtreding van Iraanse regels voor het varen door de zeestraat. Het land dreigt ook met maatregelen tegen schepen die goederen overslaan naar of van deze tankers. Voor het uitbreken van het conflict in de regio ging ongeveer een vijfde van de wereldwijde olie en aardgas door de Straat van Hormuz. clusters.headline: After 6 months of war, why aren't oil prices even higher?

items.title: After 6 months of war, why aren't oil prices even higher?
items.summary: For decades, the potential closure of the Strait of Hormuz has been considered the ultimate doomsday scenario for global oil markets. So, when Iran effectively closed the Strait earlier this year in response to the joint U.S.-Israeli assault, many analysts warned that oil prices could skyrocket to record highs. The logic was straightforward. Prior to the war, about 20% of the global oil supply transited the Strait. A loss of supply on this scale could easily have pushed oil prices to $150 or even $200 per barrel — but it didn’t. Instead, prices peaked around $120 per barrel in April and have largely stayed below $100 since June. To understand the dynamics that have so far prevented an even higher price spike, and to get a sense of where oil supply and prices may be headed as the conflict drags on, I spoke with Rory Johnston, a leading oil markets analyst and the author of the Commodity Context blog. clusters.headline: Turns out having nukes provided the US very little leverage

items.title: Turns out having nukes provided the US very little leverage
items.summary: For decades, the United States treated the prospect of an Iranian nuclear weapon as an intolerable threat. Yet when Washington and Tehran went to war twice in roughly a year, America’s own nuclear arsenal provided remarkably little leverage. In June 2025, the United States joined Israel in attacking Iran’s nuclear facilities. Iran retaliated against Israeli territory and a U.S. air base in Qatar. The following year, a far larger U.S.-Israeli campaign killed Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and much of Iran’s senior military leadership while striking the country’s nuclear, military, energy, and transportation infrastructure. Tehran responded by attacking Israel, U.S. bases across the Persian Gulf, and regional energy infrastructure. In neither war did America’s overwhelming nuclear superiority prevent Iranian retaliation or compel Tehran to capitulate. The paradox is striking: the weapon the U.S. had long insisted Iran must never possess proved largely incapable of shaping Tehran’s calculations, or determining the course of a war of choice that has consumed Trump’s presidency. items.summary: US senator criticises economic 'D-Day' against Iran, says 'Trump is losing' US Senator Chris Murphy has criticised the White House’s new sanctions on Iran, warning that American citizens are "paying a huge, huge cost" for the decision. "'D-Day' is desperate window dressing. Iran is winning the war. Trump is losing. And Americans are paying a huge, huge cost," he said in a post on X. In a series of posts, Murphy went onto list a number of reasons for Washington's setbacks during its war on Iran, including not achieving initial war objectives, Tehran's control of the strategic Strait of Hormuz and the depletion of army resources, including its munition supply. "The bottom line: Trump lost the military campaign. And now he's desperate so in his humiliating defeat, he's selling this fake economic pressure to keep up the impression we are still fighting," the US senator added. "But the war is basically over. items.title: The wars in Ukraine and Iran are becoming dangerously enmeshed | Christopher S Chivvis
items.summary: As the Trump administration refuses to end its war in Iran, it is steering into the storm, not out of it Russia hasn’t yet killed large numbers of Europeans outside Ukraine, but it’s getting closer. The night of 4-5 August, an airport bus driver discovered an armed drone lying near the tarmac of the Leipzig-Halle airport, which is a central hub of Europe’s logistical support to Ukraine’s war effort. A cargo jet, meanwhile, may have struck a second drone shortly after takeoff, forcing an abrupt landing, and investigators found a third drone laden with military explosives nearby. In 2024, incendiary devices hidden in parcels ignited in DHL cargo at the same airport. Had these detonated in the air, a major air catastrophe and large-scale civilian casualties would have ensued, probably resulting in a broader war. Continue reading...

items.title: ‘I would rather die than return to France’: the brutal reality of the UK’s one in, one out scheme
items.summary: Aso and Baran fled Iran, crossed the Channel together and were both returned to France. After risking their lives to reach Britain again, the friends found themselves facing very different fates At the end of last year, two men fled Iran. Aso and Baran* were strangers at the time. The way their stories would cross, then diverge, reveals the cruel arbitrariness of the UK asylum system in general, and the government’s controversial one in, one out scheme in particular. Before he left Iran, Aso, 28, had converted from Islam to Christianity, putting his life in imminent danger. “I had to keep my conversion to Christianity a secret,” he says. “I knew if I was caught, I risked being executed by the Iranian regime … one of my relatives, who I trusted, paid smugglers to get me out last November.” Continue reading...

items.title: Iran urges UN action over deadly US attack on wedding
items.summary: Iran urges UN action over deadly US attack on wedding Iran has accused the United States of committing a “war crime” by bombing a wedding gathering in southern Hormozgan province. In a letter to the United Nations Security Council, Iranian Ambassador Gholamhossein Darzi described the attack on civilians as an “appalling” and “egregious” crime that violated international law. Darzi urged the UN to “hold the United States fully responsible” and ensure it brings “an end to its acts of aggression” against Iran. The US strike killed at least four people, including two children, and wounded 50 others at the wedding in Sirik. Iran’s Health Ministry said recent US air strikes had killed at least 18 people and wounded another 142.

items.title: 'Inappropriate to say': Trump may still be considering CIA-led uprising in Iran
items.summary: 'Inappropriate to say': Trump may still be considering CIA-led uprising in Iran US President Donald Trump on Wednesday said it "wouldn't be appropriate to say" if he would greenlight the CIA arming Iranians to encourage a violent uprising, a day after he asked on his TruthSocial account, "When are the Iranian people going to rise up and fight?" Trump was taking unscheduled questions in the Oval Office, after the US unleashed a barrage of strikes on Iran's southern coast on Tuesday, killing 18 people, including two children at a wedding. "Will you send the CIA in to arm Iranians?" a reporter asked the president. "I'd love to tell you that, but it wouldn't be appropriate to say," Trump responded. "But I mean, I understand their plight. They're being shot... They have close to 65,000 protesters killed." It remains unclear where that figure is sourced, given Trump has previously floated figures between 25,000 and 80,000 during the anti-government protests in Iran early this year. Read more: 'Inappropriate to say': Trump may still be considering CIA-led uprising in Iran

items.title: Creating a 'NATO of Nations' in order to save it
items.summary: This summer the Pentagon handed NATO members a questionnaire asking whether they support in part, “U.S. foreign policy priorities.” Dubbed a “loyalty test” in the press, it was seen by many Europeans as the most recent sign that the alliance is coming apart because of American petulance. Yet what is actually happening is that the U.S. is putting stress on an inherently flawed and now exhausted form of alliance politics. The roots of the present discord were planted not in the 2024 reelection of President Donald Trump, but in the moment of NATO's Cold War triumph thirty years earlier. Indeed, one of the more puzzling developments after the dissolution of both the Soviet Union and the Warsaw Pact was the conviction of Western leaders that the time was ripe for new, grand projects of expansion and integration. "The secretary-general is deeply alarmed by reports of civilian casualties, including a strike that reportedly hit a wedding ceremony in Iran," UN spokesperson Stephane Dujarric said during a news conference. "The secretary-general condemns all attacks against civilians," Dujarric said. "He recalls that all parties must respect their obligations under international humanitarian law, including the principles of distinction, proportionality, and precaution." He added that the UN chief urged Washington and Tehran to "return urgently to diplomacy," adding that a "comprehensive and durable settlement can be achieved only through dialog and negotiations".

"Will you send the CIA in to arm Iranians?" a reporter asked the president. "I'd love to tell you that, but it wouldn't be appropriate to say," Trump responded. "But I mean, I understand their plight. They're being shot... They have close to 65,000 protesters killed." It remains unclear where that figure is sourced, given Trump has previously floated figures between 25,000 and 80,000 during the anti-government protests in Iran early this year. items.title: Trump’s Saudi nuke agreement may prolong the Iran war
items.summary: A final deal between the United States and Iran is slipping further out of reach. Since the Memorandum of Understanding collapsed in July, the prospects for reviving it have deteriorated by the day. While Tehran publicly demands a return to the MOU, Trump’s current position is that even if Iran reopened the Strait of Hormuz, he would neither return to the agreement nor lift the blockade on Iran. And even in the unlikely event that he did, the MOU could not come back into force as long as Israel continues to bombard Lebanon. Iran is unlikely to accept an MOU minus Lebanon: its demand for a regional ceasefire is non-negotiable. But even if these obstacles were resolved, profound differences over the nuclear issue would remain. And those differences have now grown dramatically more severe because of Trump’s nuclear agreement with Saudi Arabia. items.summary: Fair to say the current sell-off is international, but the PM has said little yet to make investors rethink the UK’s status It’s too soon to say the bond markets have turned on Andy Burnham. Tuesday’s spike in gilt yields, taking the UK’s 30-year borrowing costs to their highest level since 1998 , was part of an international sell-off of government debt . The main contributors are well known. The Iran war, by increasing the cost of energy, has overturned the comforting start-of-the-year thesis of falling global inflation and interest rates. A plunging Japanese yen has kicked away another assumed source of financial stability. The US treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, hasn’t calmed nerves with his solo, and so far futile, attempt to bring down US yields . Meanwhile, the early stage of the AI revolution is an exercise in issuing squillions of debt before long-term returns on capital can possibly be assessed meaningfully. Continue reading...

items.title: Oorlog Midden-Oosten leidt tot stuk meer aanvragen bij Nationaal Warmtefonds
items.summary: Het Nationaal Warmtefonds heeft tot nu toe al meer leningen verstrekt dan in heel 2025. Bij het fonds kunnen mensen geld lenen om hun huis te verduurzamen. Van januari tot en met augustus werden ruim 22.000 leningen verstrekt. In heel 2025 waren dat er 21.000. De lening wordt gebruikt voor bijvoorbeeld muur- en dakisolatie, isolerend glas of zonnepanelen. De piek heeft te maken met de oorlog in het Midden-Oosten, die de VS en Israël eind februari ontketenden met hun aanvallen op Iran. Als tegenzet gooide Iran de Straat van Hormuz dicht, de zeestraat waardoor tot die tijd een vijfde van de wereldwijde olie en aardgas werd vervoerd. Door die blokkade zijn de energieprijzen fors gestegen. "De piek was vanaf het moment dat de oorlog begon", vertelt Katinka Huiberts, bestuurslid bij het Nationaal Warmtefonds. "De aanvragen begonnen toen heel scherp te stijgen." Die stijging zette het hele voorjaar tot de zomer door, zegt Huiberts. items.title: Why are so many Vance allies leaving the administration?
items.summary: Army Secretary Dan Driscoll resigned this week, raising a flurry of questions about whether his departure is part of a larger political reordering that has pushed skeptics of President Donald Trump’s war policies to the margins. A long-time friend of Vice President JD Vance, Driscoll drew widespread praise for his efforts to modernize the Army. But he has clashed with Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, particularly over the latter’s firing of numerous senior military officials , including Army and Air Force generals and the Secretary of the Navy. Driscoll brought his concerns about these firings directly to Trump last week, who said he was unaware of how many officers had been purged, according to the Atlantic. Driscoll’s departure is the latest in a string of recent high-profile exits by Vance’s allies and ideological fellow travelers, including Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard, Deputy National Security Adviser Andy Baker, White House Director of Legislative Affairs James Braid, and Director of the National Counterterrorism Center Joe Kent. items.summary: El agua es una vulnerabilidad estratégica, un hecho que no es ninguna novedad para los mandos militares. Más recientemente, las infraestructuras hidráulicas han sido un objetivo importante en el conflicto de Estados Unidos con Irán, a pesar de que las leyes internacionales clasifican este tipo de ataques como posibles crímenes de guerra. En marzo, Donald Trump amenazó con «destruir por completo… posiblemente todas» las instalaciones de desalinización de Irán, que son esenciales para la vida en las áridas provincias del sur del país. Irán afirma que una de esas instalaciones fue bombardeada en la isla de Qeshm. items.title: IAEA reports progress in Syria investigation, none in Iran
items.summary: IAEA reports progress in Syria investigation, none in Iran The UN nuclear watchdog has resolved its outstanding questions in its investigation into past, secret nuclear activities in Syria under the Assad family's rule, a confidential report by the agency seen by Reuters said on Tuesday. A separate, quarterly International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) report on Iran also sent to member states and seen by Reuters showed there had again been no progress in Iran, where its lack of access to verify uranium stocks since US and Israeli attacks in June 2025 remained a "proliferation concern". items.title: Grote aanbieders verhogen de benzineprijs morgen naar nieuwe recordhoogte
items.summary: De adviesprijs voor een liter benzine bereikt woensdag zeer waarschijnlijk een nieuwe recordhoogte van rond de 2,668 euro. Dat bevestigt consumentencollectief UnitedConsumers na berichtgeving van nu.nl. Het oude record was van begin mei dit jaar: 2,646 euro. Vandaag steeg de prijs al naar net daaronder: 2,64 euro. Morgen stijgt de benzineprijs dus verder. UnitedConsumers berekent de gemiddelde adviesprijs dagelijks op basis van de prijzen van de vijf grote aanbieders: Shell, BP, Texaco, Esso en TotalEnergies. Vier van de vijf hebben hun prijs voor woensdag al doorgegeven. "Die vijfde gaat niet veel afwijken van de anderen, dus het record gaat er zeker aan", zegt Derk Foolen van UnitedConsumers. Weg van de snelweg goedkoper Wat de precieze prijs wordt, weten we morgen dus pas. "Maar 2,668 is een goede inschatting", aldus Foolen. De adviesprijs zie je vooral bij tankstations langs de snelweg. items.title: Gulf states struggle to recover economically after 6 months of war
items.summary: The Persian Gulf’s extraordinary wealth has long rested on an assumption of stability. The past six months of war have shattered that certainty, exposing a fundamental weakness in Gulf economic models: producing oil and gas is only half the equation when infrastructure and access to global markets can be disrupted. Ports, airports, power grids, desalination plants, financial centers, and tourism hubs are all vulnerable to the same regional shocks. The energy sector is particularly exposed, with damaged oil and gas facilities potentially taking months or longer to repair. Yet restoring production may prove easier than restoring confidence that Gulf exports can reliably reach global markets. Each Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) state enters this new era from a different starting point. Qatar, Kuwait and Bahrain are particularly exposed because of their reliance on Gulf maritime routes, including the Strait of Hormuz. items.title: Vance says Trump Kharg post was 'message' to Iran
items.summary: Vance says Trump Kharg post was 'message' to Iran US Vice President JD Vance has said that President Donald Trump was sending a message to Iran when he posted an AI-generated video that appeared to show the US military blowing up oil facilities on Iran's Kharg Island earlier on Monday. "The president likes to switch it up on social media a little bit," Vance said when asked about Trump's post at a press conference. "He would be the first to say he doesn't make announcements about military actions on social media, but I think that he's sending a message to the Iranians," he added. Earlier on Monday, Hamid Bovard, the chief executive of the National Iranian Oil Company, denied that the US had destroyed oil facilities on Kharg.

items.summary: Araghchi blames ‘serpent’ Netanyahu for luring Washington into war on Iran Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian has said that Tehran will respond decisively to further attacks following the US bombing of Larak Island, which killed and wounded Iranian civilians and soldiers. Speaking on Monday before travelling to Bishkek for a Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit, Pezeshkian said Iran “is not looking for war” but would “never sit still in the face of any aggression”. Iran “will give a decisive response to the aggressors” if attacked again, he said, according to the Fars news agency. “Instability and unrest in the region are not in the interest of any country and will challenge everyone,” he added. US forces bombed Larak Island on Sunday, the official state broadcaster IRIB reported. It marked Washington’s first attack on Iran since July and raised fears of another escalation in the Israeli -US war against the country . items.title: Why the Gulf Monarchies Will Not Turn Away from the United States Despite the Iran War
items.summary: The signing on 7 August of the so-called Mecca Pact by Saudi Arabia, Türkiye and Pakistan again raises the question of whether the Gulf monarchies might seek to reduce their security dependence on the United States. The Gulf monarchies’ experience of the Iran war makes such a realignment appear plausible. Despite their decades-long partnership with Washington, they became targets of Iranian drone and missile attacks that caused considerable damage to the region’s energy infrastructure and severely disrupted energy exports, as the Strait of Hormuz was effectively closed. The Trump administration appears to have taken little account of their security interests . Nevertheless, three factors make an end to their close ties with Washington unlikely. Limits of realignment First, the Gulf monarchies have no viable alternative to the United States as a security guarantor. For all their differences in foreign and security policy, they share a common predicament: None of their other partners is willing or able to take Washington’s place. The Trump administration also tacitly endorsed a multilateral, Saudi-led maritime initiative to protect shipping in the Red Sea, sending senior U.S. military officials to the meeting where the arrangement was agreed to. items.title: La modernité de l’Iranienne Forough Farrokhzâd, poétesse rebelle et lumineuse
items.summary: Forough Farrokhzâd est l’une des plus grandes figures de la poésie iranienne du dernier siècle. Sa disparition brutale en 1967, à l’âge de 32 ans, fut une perte immense pour son pays, pour la littérature. Sa voix, « fusionnée dans les atomes du temps » comme elle l’a écrit, continue de se faire entendre à travers sa poésie sublime et tragique. « J’irai jusqu’au rivage du soleil » est le titre du volume en traduction française de ses poésies complètes, paru cette année dans la prestigieuse collection Poésie/Gallimard.

items.title: Iran parliament speaker says new regional pacts can 'herald a new stage’
items.summary: Iran parliament speaker says new regional pacts can 'herald a new stage’ Iran’s parliament speaker, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, has said that new regional treaties can herald a new stage in which Muslim neighbours rely on their own capacities rather than on foreigners, according to Tasnim News Agency. In his message Saturday to mark the Unity Week, Ghalibaf described new regional treaties and arrangements as a “new chapter” and stressed that unity among Muslims has “helped push back against hegemonic ambitions”, according to Tasnim News Agency. He said these treaties show that Muslim neighbours “can choose the path of cooperation and brotherhood”, rather than “pursuing exhausting rivalries”. Ghalibaf added that recent developments have demonstrated the benefits of Muslim unity, and expressed hope that the Muslim world “would move toward greater unity, independence, security and dignity, with Muslims determining their own future free from foreign interference”.

items.title: Iran-backed Iraqi group sets 10 conditions for disarmament, including full US withdrawal
items.summary: Iran-backed Iraqi group sets 10 conditions for disarmament, including full US withdrawal Kataib Sayyid al-Shuhada, an Iran -backed Iraqi armed group, said on Saturday it will only cooperate with efforts to bring weapons under state control if 10 conditions are met, including a complete withdrawal of US forces from Iraq. The group said US forces must fully withdraw by land, sea and air, that any American presence “under any title” must end, and that Iraqi airspace must not be used to launch attacks on neighbouring countries. It also called for full federal control over Iraqi territory, stronger Iraqi-operated air defences with advanced systems, and the withdrawal of Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK) fighters and Turkish troops from northern Iraq. It said that the PKK's presence gives Turkey a pretext for cross-border operations. The group, which has longstanding ties to Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), made its statement as the Iraqi government faces a 30 September deadline to bring all armed factions' weapons under state control.

items.title: Iran will neither forgive nor forget Minab school massacre, Araghchi says
items.summary: Iran will neither forgive nor forget Minab school massacre, Araghchi says Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, has said that his country will neither forgive nor forget the Minab school massacre “but will continue to pursue it”, IRNA reported. During a visit to the “Minab School” painting exhibition on Friday, Araghchi said human rights have “become a political tool in the hands of some Western states”, “exploiting them for political gain and attaching no real value to the concept”. “We believe in human rights in the true sense of the word in Iran and have always defended the rights of the Iranian people and will not allow it to be abused by others,” he added, according to IRNA. In February, a double strike on a girls' school in Minab in southern Iran killed 165 people, mostly students aged seven to 12. Local officials say about 170 girls were at the school during the attack, which Iran attributes to the US and Israel.

items.title: US cuts off major Egyptian bank from global financial system
items.summary: US cuts off major Egyptian bank from global financial system The US Treasury on Friday announced plans to cut off Banque Misr's branches in the United Arab Emirates from the global financial system, as the Trump administration seeks to "asphyxiate" what it said were Iran's "enablers". Banque Misr is Egypt's second-largest bank. Its Emirati arm will no longer be able to do business in US dollars as of 28 September, under the new plans. The 30-day notification period is open for public comment, a process whereby the US government solicits messages of support or opposition that could potentially sway the decision. "The US Department of the Treasury’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) proposed a rule that would revoke Banque Misr UAE’s correspondent banking access to US financial institutions. Treasury assesses that Banque Misr UAE is a critical node for the Iranian regime’s access to U.S. dollars," the Treasury said. items.summary: This week, President Donald Trump formally submitted the U.S.-Saudi civil nuclear agreement to Congress for review, moving the deal forward despite continuing to insist that Saudi Arabia normalize relations with Israel before it can take effect. This condition could stall the agreement indefinitely: Riyadh demands a clear pathway toward Palestinian statehood before normalization, and Israel is dead set against statehood. Israel had strongly opposed the deal as originally negotiated, while Netanyahu had privately expressed hopes of delivering “ the next big thing ” by securing Saudi normalization before Israel’s October elections. Former U.S. Ambassador to Saudi Arabia Michael Ratney described Trump as inserting normalization “ at the last minute ,” throwing the agreement into uncertainty. Trump’s decision to submit the agreement for congressional review further adds to this uncertainty. The president appears to want it both ways: his latest move is signaling to Riyadh that the agreement is moving forward even as he assures Tel Aviv that the deal is contingent on normalization. items.title: Rachel Roddy’s recipe for saffron and tomato rice | A kitchen in Rome
items.summary: Laborious to harvest and extortionately priced, the sunset-coloured stigmas of the saffron crocus have an extraordinarily warm, pungent taste. Fortunately, however, a little goes a very long way … The saffron crocus has six lilac-purple flowers, three yellow stamens and three orange-red stigmas that extend beyond the petals like the wiry antennae of an insect. The thread-like stigmas have to be picked only by hand when the flowers are fully open, a laborious, finickety job that hasn’t changed much since ancient times. Then, to avoid the colour and flavour fading, the stigmas need to be dried very quickly, a process that reduces their weight by about 80%. Tens of thousands of fiery-looking filaments are required to produce half a kilogram of the dried threads, which make the “hay” or powder we know as saffron and explains the exorbitant cost. Fortunately, just a few threads of this precious spice go a long way. Native to Crete, Iran and south-west Asia, the saffron crocus has been cultivated since the dawn of civilisation for its medicinal properties, as well as for use in cosmetics,

items.title: Trump's war and tariffs are having a nasty effect on interest rates
items.summary: Over the last month, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has engaged in two controversial and rare interventions in financial markets. The first came in early August when the U.S. Treasury joined the government of Japan in its efforts to strengthen the yen by buying the Japanese currency, taking a step it had last taken during the Asian Financial Crisis in 1998. And late last week, Bessent announced that the Treasury could double the amount of long-dated Treasuries that it will buy back from current holders. Last February, Bessent said the administration was focused on lowering bond yields. Hegseth’s statement comes after Washington imposed “unprecedented” sanctions on Iran this week. In an interview on US cable channel Newsmax, Hegseth said “economic pressure we know hurts them the most right now, but by no means are we foreclosing using kinetic strikes anywhere in the Strait of Hormuz”.

items.title: Iran’s nuclear chief says attacked nuclear sites not secure for IAEA inspection
items.summary: Iran’s nuclear chief says attacked nuclear sites not secure for IAEA inspection Iran’s nuclear chief Mohammad Eslami said on Wednesday that the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) would not be able to inspect the country's nuclear sites that have suffered attacks in recent months until it develops a specific inspection protocol for such sites and their security is ensured, adding that Iran is still in a wartime situation, in comments carried by Iran’s IRNA news agency. Eslami said that Trump's threats to bomb the alleged secret Iranian nuclear site show the IAEA are pawns of the US and Israel, and accused the countries of pressuring the IAEA for an inspection.

In their essay, which was the basis of the book of the same name that appeared the next year, Mearsheimer and Walt had been careful to distinguish the Israel lobby from a lobby by and for Jews, but it was to no avail in the furor that the essay and book provoked. So does their contention that the policies promoted by Israel and its lobby are not in America's interest. To be sure, her self-confessed lack of foreign policy experience or even knowledge won’t be a bad thing for Trump. El problema es que cumplir con ese plan tiene un problema: requiere de una confrontación directa con China, el gran sustento de Irán. Y Trump tendrá que hacer equilibrios entre lograr un verdadero aislamiento de Irán y no abrir un nuevo frente con Pekín.Trump y su secretario del Tesoro, Scott Bessent , han hablado de ello en las últimas semanas, en una indicación de su intención de dejar de lado -al menos, de momento- la presión militar y centrarse en la presión económica. Es el tercer giro del conflicto con Irán, que ha pasado de la guerra total a la ofensiva diplomática -sin gran éxito- y, ahora, a la presión económica. items.title: Iranians queue for petrol after US announces new sanctions
items.summary: Iranians queue for petrol after US announces new sanctions Long queues formed at petrol stations across Tehran on Tuesday after the United States announced fresh sanctions targeting Iran, AFP reported. The new measures come as Washington seeks to increase economic pressure on Tehran after six months of war that has reached a military stalemate, with peace talks stalled and most traffic through the strategically important Strait of Hormuz blocked. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Monday outlined plans for what he called the “economic asphyxiation” of Iran, saying the objective was to “sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime”. According to AFP, Iranian authorities have largely shrugged off Washington’s threats, noting that the country has lived under US sanctions for decades. But residents in Tehran expressed concern that the latest measures could further affect fuel supplies and the wider economy. The queues at petrol stations came amid growing uncertainty over fuel availability and prices as the latest US measures add to economic pressure on Iran.

items.title: US economic D-Day sanctions: 'Repeated bombing attacks across Iran failed to change the calculus'
items.summary: Genie Godula is pleased to welcome Imran Bayoumi, Deputy Director & Resident Fellow at the Atlantic Council. But its effectiveness rests on several unresolved assumptions. Iran, meanwhile, has decades of experience curtailing sanctions and is again threatening regional escalation.

"We staan nu gevaarlijk dicht bij het overschrijden van een morele rode lijn: het autonoom aanvallen van mensen door machines", zeggen de VN-secretaris-generaal Antonio Guterres en de voorzitter van het Internationale Comité van het Rode Kruis, Mirjana Spoljaric. Verboden onder internationaal recht Een van de zorgen van de twee organisaties is dat machines veranderende omstandigheden niet zouden kunnen herkennen. Het aanvallen van burgers en civiele infrastructuur in conflictgebieden is verboden onder het internationaal humanitair recht, maar het kan moeilijk zijn om te bepalen wie burgers zijn in een conflictgebied. Bovendien is de vraag of machines zouden kunnen herkennen wanneer iemand zich overgeeft of wanneer een burger per ongeluk een vijandig gebied in is gekomen, aldus de organisaties. Téhéran, de son côté, maintient sa pression sur le détroit d’Ormuz, voie de navigation stratégique pour l’économie mondiale. Mais la dimension militaire demeure aussi très présente. L’Iran a développé une nouvelle stratégie, plus offensive, sans toutefois renoncer à la voie diplomatique.

items.title: China warns US against expanding Iran sanctions to Chinese firms
items.summary: China warns US against expanding Iran sanctions to Chinese firms China has warned Washington that it will retaliate if the Trump administration significantly expands its Iran-related secondary sanctions against Chinese companies. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced measures on Monday targeting companies in mainland China and Hong Kong. Washington stopped short of sanctioning major Chinese financial institutions. “China will take all necessary measures to firmly safeguard its rights and interests,” a Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson said on Tuesday. “China has made clear on many occasions its firm opposition to illicit unilateral sanctions that have no basis in international law or the authorisation of the UN Security Council,” they said. “The pressing task is to facilitate de-escalation of the situation and return to dialogue and negotiation as soon as possible,” they added.

items.title: After 6 months of war, why aren't oil prices even higher?
items.summary: For decades, the potential closure of the Strait of Hormuz has been considered the ultimate doomsday scenario for global oil markets. So, when Iran effectively closed the Strait earlier this year in response to the joint U.S.-Israeli assault, many analysts warned that oil prices could skyrocket to record highs. The logic was straightforward. Prior to the war, about 20% of the global oil supply transited the Strait. A loss of supply on this scale could easily have pushed oil prices to $150 or even $200 per barrel — but it didn’t. Instead, prices peaked around $120 per barrel in April and have largely stayed below $100 since June. To understand the dynamics that have so far prevented an even higher price spike, and to get a sense of where oil supply and prices may be headed as the conflict drags on, I spoke with Rory Johnston, a leading oil markets analyst and the author of the Commodity Context blog. items.title: Turns out having nukes provided the US very little leverage
items.summary: For decades, the United States treated the prospect of an Iranian nuclear weapon as an intolerable threat. Yet when Washington and Tehran went to war twice in roughly a year, America’s own nuclear arsenal provided remarkably little leverage. In June 2025, the United States joined Israel in attacking Iran’s nuclear facilities. Iran retaliated against Israeli territory and a U.S. air base in Qatar. The following year, a far larger U.S.-Israeli campaign killed Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and much of Iran’s senior military leadership while striking the country’s nuclear, military, energy, and transportation infrastructure. Tehran responded by attacking Israel, U.S. bases across the Persian Gulf, and regional energy infrastructure. In neither war did America’s overwhelming nuclear superiority prevent Iranian retaliation or compel Tehran to capitulate. The paradox is striking: the weapon the U.S. had long insisted Iran must never possess proved largely incapable of shaping Tehran’s calculations, or determining the course of a war of choice that has consumed Trump’s presidency. items.title: UN offers to facilitate fertiliser transit through Strait of Hormuz
items.summary: UN offers to facilitate fertiliser transit through Strait of Hormuz UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres offered on Monday to facilitate the transit of fertiliser through the Strait of Hormuz which has been disrupted as a result of the US-Israel war on Iran. “The purpose is simple: to reduce immediate risks, support more orderly and predictable transit and help rebuild the confidence necessary for diplomacy and de-escalation,” he said at a news conference. Guterres said the UN “would not authorise passage” through the strait or “alter the rights or obligations” of states under international law, but rather serve as a “neutral facilitator”, registering and verifying ships carrying fertiliser and related products. “Of course, it can only be done if the countries that are involved in this conflict all agree to accept the mechanism,” Guterres said, which would be coordinated by Oman.
